Select, then copy, in copy mode
An SSH key is a pair: a private key and a public key. The private one never leaves your device; only the public one goes on the server. Unlike a password, it cannot be guessed by trying repeatedly.
Settings \u2192 Create an SSH key, then:
1. Choose the type (Ed25519 unless you need RSA 4096 for an older server)
2. Enter a comment, such as an email address
3. The passphrase may be empty. Setting one protects the key if the device is taken
4. Create. The private key is stored encrypted here, and the public key is shown to copy
5. Add that public key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server (below)
If you already have a private key, or prefer another tool.
~/.ssh/id_ed25519 is the private key. Import that one.
Or generate one in PuTTYgen, export it in OpenSSH format, and import that.
Installing the public key on a server

Installing a public key assumes you can already get into the machine somehow. Usually one of:
• SSH with a password (an existing server, shared hosting)
• A cloud console (EC2 Instance Connect, GCP serial console, a VPS control panel)
• Direct access to a physical or virtual console (a home server, a VM)

\u26a0 This only works on a host you can still reach with a password. A host already set to key authentication (the \u201ckey\u201d badge) cannot connect, so there is nothing to install over.\n\nIf you have already switched it, set it back to Password in the host editor first.
1. Add the server from the host screen with password authentication
(if it does not exist yet, or shows the \u201ckey\u201d badge, do this first)
2. Connect and log in with the password
3. Tap the key icon on the terminal and pick the key to install
4. It will not install twice, so tapping again is harmless
5. Back on the host screen, edit it, set authentication to Private key, choose the same key, save
6. From then on it connects with the key and no password
Note: the server needs PubkeyAuthentication yes in /etc/ssh/sshd_config. Most distributions enable it by default, so try it before changing anything.
The command below carries the public key of \u201c%1$s\u201d.

If you would rather type it yourself, log in and paste this:
Public keys do not normally contain a single quote. If one does and the command fails, append it some other way than echo.
Paste the public key into the key-pair field when creating the instance,
or add it later from the console.
Settings \u2192 SSH and GPG keys \u2192 New SSH key, and paste the public key.
From a computer, `ssh-copy-id user@host` does this. The key icon in AnoTerm does the same thing over the connection you already have, which is what to use when the phone is all you have.
A passphrase encrypts the private key file itself, so someone who takes the device still cannot use the key. Worth setting on a phone. Combined with the app lock, you need not type it every time.
A private key cannot be recovered. If the device is lost or wiped, remove that public key from ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server, make a new key, and install that one.
Which is why a server that matters should keep a second way in: a password, a second key, or console access.
**Ed25519**: modern, short, strong, widely supported. Use this.
**RSA 4096**: works on old servers too. Longer.
**ECDSA**: rarely needed, except where a policy asks for it.
**OpenSSH and PEM**: AnoTerm reads both. New keys are written in OpenSSH format.
These act on the server directly. No prefix key is sent.
